headline: Red Sea tanker attacks push Brent toward $100 and drag the KSE-100 into a third straight losing session.
summary: Houthi attacks on tankers in the Red Sea and fresh US-Iran friction have pushed Brent crude to just under $100, and PSX has now fallen three sessions running -- closing 171,739 on Thursday (-1.54%) and slipping further Friday morning. The desk's macro regime flipped to risk-off this week. A real positive, S&P's sovereign upgrade to 'B', hasn't been enough to offset the oil-driven selling. With the SBP rate decision three days out (hold at 11.5% widely expected) and 6-month T-bill yields now sitting above the policy rate, the desk is leaning toward banks, E&P and fertiliser, and staying clear of OMCs, autos, cement and textile exporters.

sectors.name: Banks
sectors.why: 6-month T-bill cutoff (11.79%) is now above the 11.5% policy rate for the first time this cycle, and S&P's sovereign upgrade is a direct credit-quality tailwind for bank funding costs.

sectors.name: E&P
sectors.why: Brent holding near $100 is a direct revenue tailwind for OGDC/PPL/MARI-type producers even as the same oil move hurts importers.

sectors.name: Fertilizer
sectors.why: Domestic-demand driven with low direct oil-import exposure, so it's better insulated from the current shock than import-heavy sectors.

sectors.name: OMCs
sectors.why: June's current account swung back into deficit, and faster fuel-price pass-through on a near-$100 oil tape compounds margin-timing and circular-debt risk.

sectors.name: Autos
sectors.why: Imported-input costs rise with oil and the dollar, while inflation-pressured consumer demand caps pricing power.

sectors.name: Cement
sectors.why: Energy-cost sensitive; input-cost pressure was already visible before this fresh oil leg.

sectors.name: Textiles/exporters
sectors.why: Current account back in deficit and Red Sea/Bab-al-Mandab freight risk is now live via the Houthi tanker attacks, a direct hit to export shipping costs.

watchlist.angle: Sits at the centre of the macro desk's 'favoured' E&P call this week: Brent consolidating just under $100 after the Red Sea escalation is a direct tailwind, and E&P is a named beneficiary in this week's sector tilt.
watchlist.risk: A ceasefire or de-escalation in the Red Sea/Iran standoff would pull Brent back down fast and remove the thesis overnight.

watchlist.angle: Banks are the desk's top-favoured sector into the 2026-07-27 MPC: 6-month T-bill yields (11.79%) are now above the policy rate, and the S&P sovereign upgrade is a funding-cost tailwind for the big deposit-heavy banks.
watchlist.risk: UBL was also among Thursday's biggest single-name laggards (-2.73%) as broad risk-off selling hit banking heavyweights alongside the rest of the market.

watchlist.angle: H1 2026 results just landed with a large interim dividend and an August 5-7 book closure -- a dated, concrete catalyst in a week where most names are being sold on macro fear rather than company news.
watchlist.risk: The reported profit/dividend figures come from a single filings aggregator this cycle and haven't been cross-checked against the primary PSX/DPS filing yet.

watchlist.angle: FY26 profit +7% YoY with a confirmed Rs10/share final dividend and an August 25-31 book closure -- a real, dated catalyst, though it sits inside a sector (cement) the macro tilt currently flags as an avoid.
watchlist.risk: Cement is energy-cost sensitive; a sustained oil tape works directly against the sector even with decent underlying results.

catalysts.event: SBP Monetary Policy Committee decision -- hold at 11.5% widely expected (97% analyst poll), but T-bill yields above the policy rate make this a real one to watch
SBP post-MPC analyst briefing / Information Compendium release
PBS July 2026 CPI release -- first print to capture fuel-price pass-through from the current oil shock
NESTLE book closure opens for the interim dividend declared with H1 2026 results
BWCL book closure opens for the FY26 final dividend; AGM follows on 2026-08-31

risks: A further escalation in the Red Sea/US-Iran standoff that pushes Brent sustainably past $100 would deepen the import bill and current-account pressure that's already back in deficit.

The SBP could feel pressure to defy the hold consensus given 6-month T-bill yields are already pricing above the policy rate -- a hike would land hard on a market already three sessions into a losing streak.

The August 1 CPI print is the first to carry daily fuel-price revisions from this oil shock; a hot number would undercut the disinflation narrative that's been supporting the market's medium-term case.
disclaimer: Research, not advice. The desk generates signals; it does not place orders. Losses are expected.
